real_task_scenarios: A maintainer asks the auditor to judge whether an existing Skill can be used by the team for real work, not merely whether its Markdown is tidy.
The auditor must review a target Skill, align the real capability standard with the user, inspect content and runtime evidence, and produce a repairable readiness decision.
success_criteria: The audit finds all supported problems and risks that can make the Skill induce an agent to fail in real tasks.
The audit distinguishes instruction hygiene, attention economy, behavior induction, and capability effectiveness instead of collapsing them into structure or wording quality.
The audit asks for or records user-confirmed ability standards before formal scoring and keeps unproven safety as finding or residual risk.
The audit produces validator-backed alignment, formal report, summary, scope evidence, scorecard, content_behavior_audit, findings, repair targets, and verification hints.
failure_modes: The auditor treats repo contracts, old reports, self-description, or schema-valid JSON as proof of capability effectiveness.
The auditor over-focuses on sentence clarity and misses whether the content induces the agent to take the right actions.
The auditor calls a Skill fit while user confirmation, content behavior evidence, or failure-mode coverage remains unproven.
The auditor emits risks without concrete file-line evidence, impact, repair target, and verification path.
unacceptable_risks: A fit verdict can be produced without evidence that the user actually confirmed the ability standard.
A fit verdict can be produced by marking content behavior statuses supported without per-field evidence that the Skill content induces the required behavior.
Historical self-audit artifacts can be mistaken for current readiness proof.
evidence_requirements: P0/P1 findings must cite current path-line evidence, pass claim review, pass severity calibration, and include repair and verification hints.
Content behavior claims must be traceable to current Skill content, reference routing, validator behavior, tests, or runtime evidence.
Validator PASS proves schema and contract conformance only; semantic ability claims require direct evidence against the user-confirmed standard.
